questions.text:
At a large school, 55% of students buy their lunch from the canteen. On any given day, each student independently decides whether to buy lunch.

A group of 6 students is selected at random.

(i) State why this situation can be modelled by a binomial distribution.
(ii) Calculate the probability that exactly 4 of the 6 students buy their lunch from the canteen.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: (i) Binomial because: fixed number of trials (n = 6), two outcomes (buy/don't buy), constant probability (p = 0.55), independent trials. (ii) P(X = 4) = C(6,4) × 0.55⁴ × 0.45² = 15 × 0.09150625 × 0.2025 = 15 × 0.018530 = 0.2780. Accept 0.278.

questions.text: The school canteen manager wants to ensure there is enough food for at least 90% of the days. On a day when 200 students are at school, what is the expected number of students who buy lunch, and what is the standard deviation?
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Expected value: E(X) = np = 200 × 0.55 = 110 students. Standard deviation: σ = √(np(1-p)) = √(200 × 0.55 × 0.45) = √(49.5) = 7.04 (accept 7.04 or 7.0).

questions.text: Using your answers from Question 1b and a normal approximation, estimate the number of lunches the canteen should prepare each day to be at least 90% confident of having enough. Assume the number of students buying lunch is approximately normally distributed.
questions.markingGuide: Merit: Need P(X ≤ k) ≥ 0.90. Using normal approximation: X ~ N(110, 7.04²). The 90th percentile: z = 1.282. k = μ + zσ = 110 + 1.282 × 7.04 = 110 + 9.02 = 119.02. So the canteen should prepare at least 120 lunches (rounding up to a whole number). Must show clear working using the normal distribution.

questions.text:
Events A and B are such that P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5, and P(A ∪ B) = 0.7.

(i) Find P(A ∩ B).
(ii) Find P(A | B).
(iii) Are A and B independent? Justify your answer.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: (i) P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B), so 0.7 = 0.4 + 0.5 - P(A ∩ B), P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. (ii) P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) = 0.2/0.5 = 0.4. (iii) P(A | B) = 0.4 = P(A), so A and B ARE independent. Alternatively: P(A) × P(B) = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2 = P(A ∩ B).

questions.text:
Events C and D are mutually exclusive with P(C) = 0.3 and P(D) = 0.4.

(i) Explain why mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities cannot be independent.
(ii) Find P(C | D).
questions.markingGuide: Merit: (i) If C and D are mutually exclusive, P(C ∩ D) = 0. For independence, we need P(C ∩ D) = P(C) × P(D) = 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12. Since 0 ≠ 0.12, they cannot be independent. Intuitively: if one event occurs, the other definitely cannot, so knowing one occurred gives information about the other — the opposite of independence. (ii) P(C | D) = P(C ∩ D)/P(D) = 0/0.4 = 0.

questions.text:
A taxi company finds that the number of bookings per hour follows a Poisson distribution with a mean of 8 bookings per hour.

(i) Calculate the probability of receiving exactly 5 bookings in a given hour.
(ii) Calculate the probability of receiving 3 or fewer bookings in a 30-minute period.
(iii) The company has capacity to handle 12 bookings per hour. Find the probability that demand exceeds capacity in any given hour.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: (i) P(X = 5) = e⁻⁸ × 8⁵/5! = 0.000335 × 32768/120 = 0.000335 × 273.07 = 0.0916. Merit: (ii) In 30 min, mean = 4. P(X ≤ 3) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2) + P(3) = e⁻⁴(1 + 4 + 8 + 10.667) = 0.01832 × 23.667 = 0.4335. Accept values from tables: P(X ≤ 3) = 0.4335. Excellence: (iii) P(X > 12) = 1 - P(X ≤ 12). Using Poisson tables or calculator with λ = 8: P(X ≤ 12) ≈ 0.9362, so P(X > 12) ≈ 0.0638 (about 6.4%). The company exceeds capacity about 1 in every 16 hours.
